# What an AI engineer builds {#sec-m01}

A language model can write a polite reply in Hindi, explain a return policy, or sort a thousand complaints in a few minutes. Yet when a company puts one in front of real customers, most of the work has little to do with the model itself. This module explains why. It starts with what a model can and cannot do, and ends with a map of everything an AI engineer builds around it. That map is the plan for the rest of the book.

## What does a language model actually do?

You send it text, and it sends back text. That is all a single call to a model does.

GPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, Qwen and DeepSeek are names of models. It helps to keep three words apart. The **model** is the trained program that turns text into text. The **model provider** is the company that runs it and sells access, such as OpenAI, Google or Anthropic. The **application** is a product built on top, such as the ChatGPT app. ChatGPT is not a model; it is an application that uses OpenAI's models and adds a lot around them.

Now ask a few simple questions about what a model can do on its own.

*Ask it about an order placed this morning.* It cannot answer. A model learns from data collected up to a certain date, and knows nothing after that. It has also never seen your company's database. This limit is called the **knowledge cutoff**.

*Ask a question, then a follow-up such as "and how long will that take?"* It does not know what "that" means. Every call to a model is separate, and the model keeps nothing from one call to the next. Chat apps seem to remember because the app sends the earlier messages again with every new one. Module 4 builds this.

*Paste in three hundred pages of policy documents and a year of emails.* It will refuse, or fail. Each call accepts only a limited amount of text, called the **context window**. Module 2 explains what fills it and why a longer input does not always give a better answer.

*Ask the same question twice.* You can get two different answers. An ordinary program gives the same output for the same input, every time. A model picks its words by probability, so its output can change from one call to the next (Module 2 shows how). This is the biggest difference between AI systems and ordinary software, and much of this book deals with its effects.

*Ask it to check an order, send an email or issue a refund.* It cannot. It can only write text. It can write "I have issued your refund", but writing that sentence does not move any money.

## Three kinds of AI work

People who "work in AI" usually do one of three jobs. Some **make models**: they collect data and train models, which needs large research teams and large budgets. Some **serve models**: they make trained models run fast and cheaply on hardware, which is called inference engineering. And some **build applications**: they take a model that already exists and turn it into a product that works for real users.

This book is about the third job. You will learn enough about how models work to use them well, but you will not train a large model.

## If the model cannot act, what can?

In software, what does the actual work, such as looking up an order or sending an email? Code. A function such as `check_order_status(order_id)` can query a database and return the answer.

Can that function understand a customer who writes "mera parcel kab aayega"? No. It needs an exact order number, passed in exactly the right way. The model understands the customer perfectly, but cannot query anything. Each one has exactly what the other lacks.

So put them together. The model reads the customer's message and decides which function should run and with which values. Your program runs the function. The result goes back to the model, which writes the reply (@fig-two-halves). A model connected to functions it can ask your program to run is called an **agent**, and each such function is called a **tool**.

![A model understands language but cannot act. A tool can act but cannot understand language. Connected, the model chooses the tool and your program runs it.](/figures/m01/two-halves.pdf){#fig-two-halves}

Now look at one particular kind of tool: one that fetches information, such as a search over the company's policy documents. The model asks for the relevant paragraph, the paragraph is added to the question, and the model answers using it. That is **retrieval-augmented generation**, or **RAG**. The name describes the three steps in order: *retrieve* the information, *augment* (add to) the question with it, then *generate* the answer. RAG is not a separate technology. It is an agent whose tool fetches facts. Modules 6 to 8 are about doing it well.

You will also see agents described in other ways. "Model plus tools" came first. Then people noticed that what you put in front of the model decides most of the result, and started saying "model plus context". The newest description is "model plus harness", where the **harness** means everything around the model: the instructions, the tools, the memory, the checks, the code that runs the loop. All three descriptions are true. Building that harness is the job.

## What does an AI engineer build around the model?

@fig-system-map shows the parts, in the order a customer's message passes through them. Each part has a module of its own.

![The parts of an AI system. A message enters at the front door, is checked, is handled by the control layer with the model, its context and its tools, and is checked again on the way out. Tests, traces, cost and caching watch over everything. The numbers are the modules that cover each part.](/figures/m01/system-map.pdf){#fig-system-map}

1. **The front door** receives the message, and limits how many requests come in (Module 16).
2. **Safety checks** look at what comes in: private data, abuse, hidden instructions (Module 12).
3. **Control** decides what happens next. A fixed sequence of steps, or an agent that chooses, or a plan for a long task (Modules 11 and 14).
4. **The model** is called, perhaps several times (Modules 2 and 10).
5. **Context** decides what the model sees on each call: the instructions, the retrieved documents, the memory of the conversation (Modules 3, 4 and 6 to 8).
6. **Tools** let it act, through functions you write or through standard connectors such as MCP (Modules 5 and 13).
7. **Safety checks** look at what goes out, before the customer sees it or a refund is issued (Module 12).
8. Under all of it, **quality and operations**: tests that show whether it works, traces of every run, cost and caching, safe releases (Modules 9, 15 and 16).

The model is one box out of eight. The other seven are what the engineer builds.

## Calling a model is not calling a function

In code, a model call looks like any other function call: text goes in, text comes out. It behaves very differently.

```{=latex}
\needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

| | An ordinary function | A model call |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Microseconds | Seconds |
| Failure | Rarely fails | Fails sometimes: busy servers, limits, timeouts |
| Same input | Same output, every time | A different output is possible every time |
| Cost | Free to run | Charged for every call, by the amount of text |

Each row changes how you write code around the model. Because the output varies, you check every reply before your code uses it (Module 5), and you cannot test it the usual way (Module 9). Because calls fail, you retry some failures and not others (Module 11). Because calls are slow, you run many at once, within the provider's limits (Module 15). And because every call costs money, you count what you send (Modules 3 and 15).

## Should this problem use AI at all?

The table above gives a simple rule. A model is slower, costlier and less predictable than ordinary code. So when ordinary code can do the job, use ordinary code.

"Was this order placed more than 7 days ago?" is a date comparison. One line of code answers it correctly every time, for free. "Is this customer angry, and are they asking for a refund?", written in a mix of Hindi and English with spelling mistakes, cannot be written as a rule. That is where a model earns its cost.

Before building, ask four questions:

1. Is the input messy language, or a judgement that no rule can capture? If not, write the rule.
2. If the model is wrong, will someone notice, and how much will it cost?
3. What does success look like, as a number you can measure before and after?
4. Can you buy this ready-made? A generic support bot may be enough. You build your own when you need your own data, your own rules, or control over what it is allowed to do.

## Your first call, and what it costs

Here is a complete call to a model in Python, using Anthropic's client library. Other providers' libraries look very similar.

```python
import anthropic

MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"          # model names change; keep this in one place
client = anthropic.Anthropic()     # reads the API key from the environment

reply = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=1000,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Can I return opened earbuds after 10 days?"}],
)
for block in reply.content:
    if block.type == "text":
        print(block.text)
print(reply.usage.input_tokens, reply.usage.output_tokens)
```

The answer will be polite and sensible, and probably wrong for your shop, because the model has never seen your return policy. The last line prints how much text went in and came out, counted in **tokens**, the small pieces of text that models read and charge by. Module 2 explains what a token is.

Now work out the cost. Suppose the provider charges ₹350 for every million input tokens and ₹1,700 for every million output tokens. (These are assumed example prices. Output usually costs several times more than input, and Module 2 explains why.)

1. This question was about 30 tokens in and 120 tokens out: 30 × 350 ÷ 10,00,000 + 120 × 1,700 ÷ 10,00,000, about ₹0.21.
2. A real support request also carries instructions and the relevant part of the policy: say 3,000 tokens in and 300 out. That is 1.05 + 0.51, about ₹1.56 per message.
3. At 4,000 messages a day, that is about ₹6,240 a day, or about ₹1,87,000 a month.

Two things stand out. Most of the cost comes from the text sent *with* each question, not from the question itself. And the bill grows with every message, so a small saving per call becomes a large saving per month. Modules 3 and 15 come back to both.

## The project for this book

Through the book, you will build one system: a customer-support agent for **Tarkika**, an imagined online marketplace that sells phones, electronics, fashion and home products across India. By the end, it will:

- answer questions from the company's policy documents, with the source of each answer, and say "I don't know" when the documents do not cover a question;
- look up orders, and prepare refunds that a person approves above a set amount;
- remember a customer's earlier messages, and keep each customer's data separate;
- refuse hidden instructions in customer emails;
- report its own quality, cost and speed.

Each of these is one part of @fig-system-map. The first thing to understand is the model in the middle: how it reads text, why the same question can get different answers, and why you pay for every piece of text you send. That is Module 2.
